chapter: Jack Laine and the New Orleans scene
title: Parade bands, the knife fight with Pansy Laine, and boxing
summary: Street bands at carnival, his fight with Pansy, who cut him, and his training with local boxers.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs

blocks.x: Jack Lane's, you were with Jack Lane's outfit here in the audience, playing there, and he had all that bunch of bands. You would march too? You marched with the bands? Oh, yes. But you see, they never did put all

the kids together in the street band that I can remember. Discount them through? Yes. Carnival time, Jack Lane had rolled practically all of the bands that he could gather together to make it, see. And, uh, that's all they played was Dixieland, because that's all they knew. Uh-huh. Nothing else. Well,
then, for dance, it's the same thing. They split them up, the kids? Oh, no. Sometimes all the kids played

with, uh, possibly two grown-ups, the old man Lane, Jack. Uh, I remember when, when I had a fight with Pansy on the Canal Street Fern. You see, he cut this, see that cut? Yeah, you told me about that. How'd that happen? Well, he, he was looking for trouble, and I tried to give it to him. Before I could put it on his jaw, he ripped me with a knife. I didn't know he had a knife. Well, you're damn lucky you didn't cut your tendons, man. Well, I was lucky, because I had this hand straight up. Of course, in those days, I could fight, too, and he knew it. So, I guess that's why he came after me with the knife. He wouldn't have stood a chance as far as, uh, battling was concerned, because I worked out with all of these fighters around here. I used to work out with Kid Greaves and Joe Mandots. All, all the good fighters down there along in J.C. What was your weight then? 126? No, I read, yeah, that's around the featherweight limit, but I, I had, uh, one fight, and then my mother told Louis Bernier that, uh, you fought professionally one time? Yeah, I used to go down and take a beating every day after school, but I learned to fight. I learned to protect myself. Uh, I used to, uh, train with the champion Phantom of the South, Jack Hurley. He later became a great fighter. Well, he was then, too, when I worked with him. He taught me lots, and, well, I didn't, I tell you, if my folks would let me go, I might have been, uh, been the featherweight champion of the world. Yeah. Because I got so working out with these different fellas that it was a question of defend yourself or take it, and I didn't want to get hit any more oftener than, uh, than was necessary. Yeah, you know how many of them were walking on their heels, all those good things. Oh, yeah, but they couldn't hit me solid. None of them hit me solid. None of them ever knocked me down, and, and I worked out with those fellas for about two years. I loved it, liked to fight. So, after a while, my mother, I had me all sewed up with Louis Buenier while they bored me out of the place. I decided that I did gain something out of the whole experiment anyway, because of the fact that I could fight. I could defend myself. I never went around looking for any trouble with anybody, uh, but when, uh, anybody looked for trouble with me, they got it. You know, uh, uh, Pansy played a con, man? Uh, Pansy Lane, he played drums at that time. He did? Oh, yeah, it was years and years later before he ever took a, he used to play, uh, he used to play, uh, peck horn, yeah, he played in the band.
